summary:
AstroHealth is a visual health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions. It is a web app that installs and runs like a native app on cell phones, tablets, and computers via a single link, without requiring an app store. A service worker stores a copy of the app on the device so it can work offline (such as aboard a spacecraft) and continues to provide everything the crew needs, built with pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with an interface in English and Spanish. It allows users to track 12 indicators (heart rate, oxygen levels, sleep, radiation, stress, etc.) and 12 symptoms using the keyboard, mouse clicks, and a pulse measurement via screen taps.

It displays a health score (0–100), color-coded cards, a body map with 10 interactive regions, and trend graphs. Each out-of-range value explains what it means in space and what to do, with three levels (Normal, Monitor, Critical) that indicate whether the astronaut should act alone, notify the medical officer, or send a report to the flight surgeon on Earth, taking into account the actual communication delay. It includes daily routines and gamification to encourage consistent use. Far from Earth, crews must be able to assess themselves and make decisions autonomously, and this educational prototype makes that process accessible and understandable.
details:
AstroHealth is a web-based health self-assessment application for astronauts on long-duration missions. It is a web app that installs and runs like a native app on cell phones, tablets, and computers via a single link, without requiring an app store. A service worker stores a copy of the app on the device so that when it is offline (such as aboard a spacecraft), it continues to function with everything the crew needs. The astronaut tracks 12 indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, stress, radiation dose, exercise, hydration, and body mass) and 12 symptoms. Data is entered using the keyboard, clicks (mood and stress selectors and the symptom list), and a pulse measurement via screen taps—the astronaut taps the screen with each heartbeat, and the app calculates the heart rate.

Using this data, the app calculates a health score from 0 to 100, displays color-coded cards and 7-day mini-charts, and classifies each value into three levels: Normal, Watch, and Critical. For each out-of-range value, it explains what it means in space and what actions to take. It also includes a body map with 10 interactive regions, 7-, 14-, or 30-day trend graphs, a daily routine with reminders, and a “Report to Earth” button that generates a report for the flight surgeon and simulates transmission with the actual communication delay of the selected environment.

What benefits does it offer?

  1. It works offline, just as it would aboard a spacecraft.
  2. It teaches astronauts how to monitor their health: each section explains how to measure a specific health metric and why it matters in space.
  3. It clearly indicates when to take action on your own, when to notify the crew medical officer, and when to escalate the issue to the flight surgeon.
  4. It detects trends over several days, such as accumulated sleep debt, persistent low mood, or exercise falling short of the weekly goal.
  5. It calculates cumulative radiation exposure against NASA’s career limit (600 mSv) and estimates bone loss.
  6. It encourages consistency with XP, levels, streaks, and 11 badges.
  7. It is available in English and Spanish.

What is the expected impact?

On distant missions, such as a trip to Mars, communication with Earth can take up to about 12 minutes each way, so crews must be able to assess themselves and make decisions autonomously. AstroHealth illustrates this approach and can serve as an educational foundation for future monitoring tools. Its planned next steps include measuring heart rate with the camera (finger photoplethysmography), integrating real sensors via Bluetooth (pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor, actigraph), adding a view for the medical officer showing the status of the entire crew, a clearer interface, and support for more languages.

What tools and technologies did you use?

  1. Pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, without libraries or external dependencies.
  2. Custom graphics using Canvas, human figures, and SVG icons.
  3. Local storage using localStorage, with export and import in JSON.
  4. Responsive design for desktop, tablet, and phone, with keyboard accessibility.
  5. Claude (Anthropic), used via Claude Code, as a Super Intelligence (SI) tool. It generated the code, reference data, texts, and the Spanish translation. The team chose the challenge and approach, named the product, defined the language requirements, and directed the work by requesting each change. The source files disclose the use of SI.
  6. Reference sources: NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) and the Canadian Space Agency.

In what way is it creative?

  1. It measures your heart rate without any hardware—just by tapping the screen.
  2. It turns health care into a gaming experience, with ranks, streaks, and “perfect days.”
  3. It uses an interactive body map that explains how space affects each organ.
  4. It simulates the actual communication delay for each environment (spacecraft, station, rover, base), demonstrating why autonomy is necessary.
  5. It includes a demo mission featuring a 30-day journey to Mars with simulated data.

What factors did the team take into account?

  1. Offline operation, no installation required, and data stored only in the browser.
  2. Languages: English for the judges and Spanish as an option.
  3. Five environments, each with its own gravity, typical radiation levels, exercise goals, and communication delays.
  4. The five hazards of spaceflight according to NASA: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravitational fields, and hostile and enclosed environments.
  5. Do not assume the astronaut has prior medical knowledge.
  6. Transparency: The ranges and models are educational approximations; the app is not a medical device; and the team must verify the figures in js/data.js against the sources before submission.
